How much should a locksmith charge for a service call?

A lockout or a rekey feels like a quick number to quote on the phone, and that is exactly how the after-hours premium gets forgotten and the trip fee gets folded into "just the labor." A full quote has to separate billed time from parts, apply an emergency premium to time only, and compare the result against a minimum service charge — the floor that protects a short job from pricing below what showing up cost.

Open the free locksmith bid calculator

What a phone quote usually hides

The after-hours premium, applied inconsistently. A call taken at 2am deserves a premium for your availability, not for extra difficulty — and that premium belongs on labor and travel time, never on parts, which cost the same at any hour.

Travel time billed at the wrong rate, or not billed at all. Drive time to a call is time you cannot sell to anyone else. Pricing it separately from on-site labor keeps a far call from quietly costing you more than it earns.

A callback reserve. A rekey or install occasionally needs a free return visit. Setting aside a percentage of the job's direct cost for that risk keeps it from eating into margin on every job where it happens, instead of only the ones where you remember to add it.

The minimum service charge as a real floor, not a suggestion. A five-minute job with no parts can calculate to well under $90 once you count only labor and the trip fee — a stated minimum, compared against the calculated price, is what keeps that trip from being a loss.

Worked example: an emergency lockout

A customer calls at night, locked out, 15 minutes of labor once you arrive and 25 minutes of round-trip travel, an $85/hour rate, a 50% after-hours premium, a $45 trip fee, no parts (nothing replaced), a 4% callback reserve, 15% overhead, and a 30% target margin:

FigureValue
Billed time (labor + travel, before premium)$56.67 (0.67 hrs × $85)
Emergency premium (50% of billed time)$28.33
Total billed time$85.00
Trip fee$45.00
Parts$0.00
Callback reserve (4%)$5.20
Overhead (15%)$20.28
Total cost$155.48
Price at 30% target margin$222.11
Minimum charge applied?No — $222.11 is above the $89 floor
Profit$66.63

Skip the after-hours premium on this same call and the price drops to about $173.70 — an $89 minimum still never enters the picture, but the emergency premium alone is worth roughly $48 here, money that disappears the moment a quote gets rounded to a flat "call it $180, cash" on the phone instead of built up from the two pieces. On a shorter, parts-free daytime call the same arithmetic can fall below the $89 floor entirely, which is when the minimum — not the formula — sets the price.

Common questions

How much should I charge for an emergency lockout call?

Start from your normal labor and travel time cost, add the after-hours premium to that billed time only (not to any parts), add the trip fee and a callback reserve, then apply overhead and your target margin. A 15-minute lockout with 25 minutes of travel at an $85/hr rate, a 50% emergency premium, and a $45 trip fee prices at about $222.11 once overhead and a 30% margin are applied — well above a flat $89 minimum, which is what makes the after-hours premium worth tracking separately instead of folding it into a round number.

Why would a locksmith undercharge for an after-hours call?

Because the after-hours premium is easy to apply to the whole quote in your head and easy to forget applying to travel time specifically — a call 25 minutes away at 2am costs the same drive either way, but the labor on top of it is worth more because you are giving up sleep or another evening to take it. Pricing time and parts separately, and applying the premium to time only, keeps the parts markup honest and the after-hours premium visible instead of blended away.

When does the minimum service charge matter more than the calculated price?

On short, low-parts jobs — a single cut key, a car door unlock with no hardware replaced. A five-minute job with five minutes of travel and no parts can calculate to well under $90 once you count only labor and trip fee, which is why a stated minimum service charge, compared against the calculated price, protects the trips that would otherwise price below what showing up cost.

Does this pricing guide replace checking my state's locksmith licensing rules?

No. This is pricing arithmetic only. Licensing, bonding, and insurance requirements vary by state and municipality, and verifying and maintaining them is a separate step this guide and the calculator do not cover.

Why does the after-hours premium apply to labor and travel time but not to parts?

The callback reserve sets aside a percentage of the job's direct cost to absorb that risk instead of it silently eating into margin on every job where it happens.

vs-a-flat-rate-for-every-call.html.text:
← Locksmith Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate for every call

“$X for a lockout, day or night” is not a price for a service call — it is a price for one time of day, quietly applied to every call that comes in.

What a flat rate for every call is

A flat rate is the fastest way to quote a service call over the phone: name a number and go. Customers like it because it is simple, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for a daytime, scheduled call — the kind that happens during normal business hours — and then reused for every call afterward, whether or not the next one comes in at 2am, whether or not it is over in five minutes.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter labor and travel minutes, whether the call is after-hours or emergency, parts cost and markup, a callback reserve, overhead, target margin, and a minimum service charge floor. It applies the after-hours premium to billed time only — never to parts, since a cylinder costs the same at 2am as at 2pm — and compares the calculated price against the floor, using whichever is higher. You get the price for this call, not a flat number for every call.

What a flat rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same number for a call at 2pm and a call at 2am, even though the after-hours dispatch is the reason you answered the phone at all. Applies an after-hours premium to billed time (labor + travel), as its own line, so a night call is priced for being available at night.
Has no floor — a five-minute lockout with a short drive can price below what the trip itself costs to run. Compares the calculated price against a minimum service charge and uses the higher of the two, so a quick call is never quoted below the floor.
Applies any premium it does have to the whole job, parts included. Applies the after-hours premium to billed time only — a cylinder or a fob costs the same regardless of the hour.
Gives you a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the profit margin and effective hourly rate on the price you are considering, so a shopped price can be scored before you commit to it.

The same call, two times of day

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults — 30 minutes labor, 20 minutes travel, a $90 hourly rate, a $35 trip fee, $40 in parts at a 40% markup, a 4% callback reserve, 15% overhead, and a 30% target margin:

Quoted during the day, this call costs $198.54 to run and this calculator prices it at $283.62 — the target 30% margin. The identical call — same labor, same travel, same parts — called in as an after-hours emergency dispatch costs $243.39 to run, because the 50% after-hours premium on billed time flows through the callback reserve and overhead too, and this calculator prices it at $347.69, still the target 30% margin. Quote the emergency call at the daytime flat price of $283.62 instead, and it still covers its $243.39 cost — but the margin falls to 14.19%, a $64.07 shortfall against what this calculator prices the same call at once the after-hours premium is counted. Same job, same flat rate, a third of the intended margin gone the moment the sun goes down.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate get an after-hours call wrong?

Because the cost of being available at 2am is not in the labor or the parts -- it is a separate premium on the billed time, and a flat rate has no line for it. Using this calculator's own shipped defaults (30 minutes labor, 20 minutes travel, a $90 hourly rate, a $35 trip fee, $40 in parts at a 40% markup), the identical call quoted in the daytime and quoted as an emergency dispatch cost different amounts to run, because the 50% after-hours premium on billed time flows through the callback reserve and overhead too -- the daytime call costs $198.54 to run and the emergency call costs $243.39, on the same labor, travel, and parts.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

The after-hours premium and the minimum service charge floor. A flat rate has no line that raises the price when a call comes in outside normal hours, and no floor that stops a very short call -- a five-minute lockout with a ten-minute drive -- from pricing below what the trip itself costs to run. Both protect a specific kind of call: the premium protects being available at 2am, and the floor protects the quick jobs a hard hourly rate would price too low.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults: the daytime call prices at $283.62, on a job that costs $198.54 to run, holding the target 30% margin. The identical call as an after-hours emergency dispatch costs $243.39 to run and this calculator prices it at $347.69, still the target 30% margin. Quoting the emergency call at the daytime flat price of $283.62 still covers its $243.39 cost, but the margin falls to 14.19% -- a $64.07 shortfall against what this calculator prices the same call at once the after-hours premium is counted.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote?

For calls that only ever happen during normal business hours, a flat rate can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a genuine after-hours or emergency dispatch at the same number, because the rate does not know whether the call came in at 2pm or 2am, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or parts costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's parts pricing, or what other locksmiths in your area charge. It takes labor and travel minutes, whether the call is after-hours, your parts cost and markup, a callback reserve, overhead, target margin, and your minimum service charge, and turns that into a price for this call -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Housecall Pro is field service management software for home service businesses, used as a central hub for the work around a job rather than the pricing of one. Housecall Pro's current plan names and dollar figures are not verified from this page, so none are repeated here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software, sold as an ongoing account — are stated, and no price for Housecall Pro appears anywhere on this page.

Field service platforms are built to move a job through scheduling, dispatch, invoicing and payment, and they hold whatever price book or flat-rate pricing you put into them. Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Workiz?

They do different jobs, and a mobile locksmith of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Workiz is a field service management platform, founded in 2015 by three former locksmiths (Idan Kadosh, Erez Marom, and Saar Kohanovitch) and headquartered in San Diego, California, used by locksmith, junk removal, garage door, appliance repair, and other on-demand trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, and communication across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes labor and travel minutes, an after-hours/emergency premium applied to billed time only, parts cost and markup, a callback reserve, overhead, target margin, and a minimum service charge floor, and turns that into the quote for one call — then checks whether a day's worth of calls, at that average profit, clears a daily income goal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A locksmith who already schedules calls, dispatches technicians, and invoices across a whole business is better served by Workiz or a comparable field service platform; a locksmith who wants an instant, private answer to what one call should cost before it is quoted — with the after-hours premium and the minimum charge built in — is in the right place here.
